Paper.title: Dysbiosis of a microbiota–immune metasystem in critical illness is associated with nosocomial infections
Paper.authors: Schlechte J, Willing B, Lowes D, West ML, Mager DR, Fuhr JE, Gold MR, Bhatt M
Paper.population: Adult ICU patients, University of Calgary, Canada
Paper.paper_summary: This prospective cohort study of 51 critically ill ICU patients used 16S rRNA sequencing of rectal swabs to characterize gut microbiome dynamics during the first week of critical illness. Enterobacteriaceae relative abundance was markedly elevated (~10-fold) in ICU patients compared to healthy controls and dominated compositional shifts over time. Progressive Enterobacteriaceae enrichment was independently associated with increased odds of nosocomial infection (OR 6.8) and with correlated innate immune dysregulation including elevated proinflammatory cytokines and immature neutrophil expansion.

Paper.title: Clostridioides difficile infection in pediatric inflammatory bowel disease: current understanding and clinical challenges
Paper.authors: Rogalidou M
Paper.population: Pediatric patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), including Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, and IBD-unclassified; review also covers general pediatric CDI populations
Paper.paper_summary: This 2026 narrative review by Rogalidou synthesizes current evidence on Clostridioides difficile infection in pediatric IBD, covering epidemiology, risk factors, pathogenesis, diagnostic challenges, clinical outcomes, and management strategies. It highlights that children with IBD face an approximately 11-fold increased CDI risk versus non-IBD peers, and that the CDI-IBD comorbidity substantially increases hospitalization, abdominal surgery rates (8% vs. 3% at 6 months), recurrence (25-34%), and immunosuppressive therapy escalation burden (67% of patients). This is a narrative (not systematic) review that synthesizes findings from multiple cohort studies and meta-analyses without formal pooled quantitative analysis.

Paper.title: Bloodstream infection by Lactobacillus rhamnosus in a haematology patient: why metagenomics can make the difference
Paper.authors: Mannavola CM; De Maio F; Marra J; Fiori B; Santarelli G; Posteraro B; Sica S; D'Inzeo T; Sanguinetti M
Paper.population: Single 20-year-old female with relapsed/refractory Philadelphia-negative B-cell ALL post-allogeneic HSCT
Paper.paper_summary: This case report mentions Akkermansia muciniphila in a single Discussion sentence as a novel probiotic organism that displays intrinsic glycopeptide resistance, illustrating that antimicrobial resistance profiles of probiotic species may have clinical implications for gut microbiota management. No A. muciniphila clinical data from the paper's own patient is reported.

Paper.title: Role of the Intestinal Microbiota in Resistance to Colonization by Clostridium difficile
Paper.authors: Britton RA, Young VB
Paper.study_design: narrative review — no original data; reviews animal model studies (murine and hamster CDI models), in vitro mechanistic studies, and human observational findings on the role of the gut microbiota in CDI colonization resistance
Paper.population: Not applicable (review article); cited studies use hamster/mouse models and human patients with CDI
Paper.paper_summary: This narrative review synthesizes the mechanistic basis of colonization resistance against Clostridioides difficile, covering: (1) how antibiotic-induced disruption of the indigenous gut microbiota creates conditions permitting C. difficile spore germination via bile acid pool shifts (elevated cholate, suppressed secondary bile acids); (2) the role of Lachnospiraceae loss in CDI susceptibility demonstrated by murine models; (3) competition for nutrients including host-derived sialic acids in C. difficile expansion; and (4) therapeutic restoration of colonization resistance via FMT and defined microbial communities. The paper uses the name 'Clostridium difficile' (pre-2016 nomenclature); mapped to preferred name 'Clostridioides difficile'.

Paper.title: Clostridioides difficile pathogenesis and control
Paper.authors: Chilton CH, Viprey V, Normington C, Moura IB, Buckley AM, Freeman J, Davies K, Wilcox MH
Paper.population: Not applicable (review article)
Paper.paper_summary: In this narrative review of CDI pathogenesis and control, Clostridium scindens is highlighted as a key gut commensal that directly inhibits Clostridioides difficile via 7α-dehydroxylation of primary bile acids to secondary bile acids (deoxycholic acid, lithocholic acid), which suppress C. difficile spore germination and vegetative cell outgrowth. The review identifies C. scindens as a candidate species for precision microbiome reconstitution to restore colonisation resistance against C. difficile. Supporting evidence cited within the review is from gnotobiotic mouse studies (Buffie et al. 2015, Theriot et al. 2016); no direct human clinical trial data on C. scindens is reported in this paper itself.

Paper.title: Oral Pathobiont-Derived Outer Membrane Vesicles in the Oral–Gut Axis
Paper.authors: Catalan EA, Seguel-Fuentes E, Fuentes B, Aranguiz-Varela F, Castillo-Godoy DP, Rivera-Asin E, Bocaz E, Fuentes JA, Bravo D, Schinnerling K, Melo-Gonzalez F
Paper.population: N/A
Paper.paper_summary: This narrative review synthesizes evidence on Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn) as an oral pathobiont whose outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) carry virulence factors (FadA adhesin, FomA, LPS) enabling translocation via the oral–gut axis and systemic dissemination. Fn OMVs promote colorectal carcinogenesis through Wnt/β-catenin activation and immune evasion, and are associated with inflammatory bowel disease, acute liver injury, and extra-intestinal cancers. Evidence is predominantly from murine models and in vitro studies; the review presents no primary clinical cohort data of its own.

Paper.title: Microbiota-Based Therapeutics as New Standard-of-Care Treatment for Recurrent Clostridioides difficile Infection
Paper.authors: Stallhofer J, Steube A, Katzer K, Stallmach A
Paper.population: adults with recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection (rCDI)
Paper.paper_summary: This 2024 narrative review cites Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis (listed under the common commercial name 'Bifidobacterium lactis', strains Bi-07 and Bl-04) as two of four components in a probiotic mixture evaluated in one RCT (Barker et al. 2017, n=31) for mild-to-moderate initial CDI. The mixture improved CDI infection duration and diarrhea severity but showed no significant difference in recurrence (13/15 probiotic vs 15/16 placebo). Individual strain contributions cannot be isolated; the review's overall conclusion is that probiotic evidence for rCDI remains insufficient.

Paper.title: Dietary fiber and probiotics influence the gut microbiome and melanoma immunotherapy response
Paper.authors: Spencer CN, McQuade JL, Gopalakrishnan V, McCulloch JA, Vetizou M, Cogdill AP, et al.
Paper.study_design: mixed: single observational cohort (primary) + parallel preclinical murine models
Paper.population: Germ-free C57BL/6 mice colonized with complete responder (CR) donor stool via FMT, then gavaged with B. longum 35624–based probiotic (probiotic 1), implanted with BRAF V600E/PTEN-null melanoma cells, and treated with anti-PD-L1 (n=4–5 per group for tumor growth; n=6 per group for immune profiling; n=7–8 per group for microbiome analysis)
Paper.paper_summary: Germ-free mice colonized with a complete ICB responder's microbiota and then gavaged with a Bifidobacterium longum 35624–based probiotic demonstrated significantly impaired antitumor response to anti-PD-L1 therapy, with significantly larger tumors versus sterile water control (P=0.04). The B. longum probiotic was associated with reduced gut microbiome diversity and a significantly lower frequency of IFN-γ–positive CD8+ cytotoxic T cells in the tumor microenvironment (P=0.03). These findings are entirely preclinical; the human cohort in this paper did not characterize which specific probiotic species patients used.

Paper.title: Within-host evolution of a gut pathobiont facilitates liver translocation
Paper.authors: Yang Y, Nguyen M, Khetrapal V, Sonnert ND, Martin AL, Chen H, Kriegel MA, Palm NW
Paper.population: Germ-free (GF) and specific-pathogen-free (SPF) C57BL/6 mice monocolonised with individual bacterial isolates; autoimmune-prone (NZW×BXSB)F1 mice; in vitro BMDM phagocytosis and antimicrobial peptide assays
Paper.paper_summary: This germ-free mouse monocolonization study demonstrates that Enterococcus gallinarum undergoes within-host evolution to generate mucosally-adapted lineages distinct from luminal lineages, with significantly enhanced translocation to mesenteric lymph nodes and liver. Mucosally-adapted isolates show increased resistance to lysozyme, antimicrobial peptides, and macrophage phagocytosis, driven by mutations in pgdA and the manXYZ operon affecting capsular polysaccharide production. Liver-translocating isolates exacerbate lupus-like autoimmune phenotypes in susceptible mice, and E. gallinarum has been detected in liver biopsies of human patients with autoimmune hepatitis and primary sclerosing cholangitis in prior studies cited by the authors.

Paper.authors: Li X, Arias CA, Aitken SL, Galloway Peña J, Panesso D, Chang M, Diaz L, Rios R, Numan Y, Ghaoui S, DebRoy S, Bhatti MM, Simmons DE, Raad I, Hachem R, Folan SA, Sahasarabhojane P, Kalia A, Shelburne SA

Paper.title: Gut microbiome modulates response to anti-PD-1 immunotherapy in melanoma patients
Paper.authors: Gopalakrishnan V, Spencer CN, Nezi L, et al. (Wargo JA)
Paper.population: Metastatic melanoma patients undergoing anti-PD-1 immunotherapy (n=112 total; fecal microbiome analyzed in n=43: 30 responders, 13 non-responders; WGS subset n=25: 14R, 11NR)
Paper.paper_summary: A prospective cohort study of 112 metastatic melanoma patients on anti-PD-1 therapy found that Ruminococcaceae family was significantly enriched in the gut microbiome of responders versus non-responders by 16S rRNA sequencing and LEfSe analysis (p<0.01). This paper establishes the original human evidence for Ruminococcaceae enrichment in anti-PD-1 immunotherapy responders; FMT from responders into germ-free mice further demonstrated reduced tumor growth and enhanced anti-tumor CD8+ T cell responses, supporting a causal role for a Ruminococcaceae-enriched microbiome.

Paper.title: Gut microbiome influences efficacy of PD-1-based immunotherapy against epithelial tumors
Paper.authors: Routy B, Le Chatelier E, Derosa L, Duong CPM, Tidjani Alou M, Daillère R, et al.
Paper.study_design: Multi-cohort observational metagenomics study with preclinical mouse FMT experiments
Paper.population: Advanced NSCLC (n=140), RCC (n=67), and urothelial carcinoma (n=42) patients receiving PD-1/PD-L1 blockade; metagenomics subset n=100; two validation cohorts (n=53 NSCLC+RCC and n=239 NSCLC)
Paper.paper_summary: Routy et al. demonstrate that baseline gut microbiome composition governs the efficacy of PD-1/PD-L1 immune checkpoint blockade in cancer patients. Akkermansia muciniphila was the commensal most significantly associated with clinical response in NSCLC and RCC patients across three independent cohorts, with detectable A. muciniphila in 69% of partial responders vs. 34% of progressors (P=0.007). FMT and oral gavage experiments in mouse tumor models established a causal role for A. muciniphila in restoring ICI efficacy via IL-12-dependent CCR9+CXCR3+CD4+ T cell recruitment.

Paper.title: The commensal microbiome is associated with anti-PD-1 efficacy in metastatic melanoma patients
Paper.authors: Matson V, Fessler J, Bao R, Chongsuwat T, Zha Y, Alegre ML, Luke JJ, Gajewski TF
Paper.population: Metastatic melanoma patients before anti-PD-1 immunotherapy
Paper.paper_summary: This cohort study of 42 metastatic melanoma patients collected baseline stool samples before anti-PD-1 therapy and identified commensal species associated with clinical response by integrating 16S rRNA, shotgun metagenomic, and qPCR methods. Bifidobacterium longum was among 8 species significantly enriched in responders (n=16) versus non-responders (n=26). Fecal microbiota from responding patients improved tumor control and augmented CD8+ T cell responses in germ-free mice reconstituted with human stool.

Paper.title: Gastrointestinal Dissemination and Transmission of Staphylococcus aureus following Bacteremia
Paper.authors: Kernbauer E, Ding Y, Cadwell K
Paper.population: C57BL/6 mice; intravenous bacteremia model with wild-type, agr mutant, sae mutant, and agr+sae double-mutant S. aureus strains; n=5–10 mice per group; transmission experiments n=6 recipient mice
Paper.paper_summary: A murine bacteremia model demonstrating that S. aureus disseminates from the bloodstream to the gastrointestinal tract after intravenous infection, resulting in intestinal colonization and sustained fecal shedding. Fecal-oral transmission to naive cage-mates was demonstrated and required intact agr and sae virulence regulatory systems (10³-fold reduction with agr+sae double mutant). In oxacillin-treated mixed infections (MRSA + MSSA), MRSA strains were selectively transmitted to antibiotic-naive recipients, establishing that the fecal-oral route drives antibiotic-resistant strain spread under selective pressure.

Paper.title: c-Maf-dependent regulatory T cells mediate immunological tolerance to a gut pathobiont
Paper.authors: Xu M, Pokrovskii M, Ding Y, Yi R, Au C, Harrison OJ, Galan C, Belkaid Y, Bonneau R, Littman DR
Paper.study_design: murine experimental study — TCR transgenic mice, conditional knockout models (Maf^ΔTreg, Rorc^ΔTreg, Gata3^ΔTreg, Il10^-/-), adoptive T cell transfer, flow cytometry, RNA-seq
Paper.population: Mouse (C57Bl/6 background), colonized with H. hepaticus ± SFB; 4–21 animals per group across multiple independent experiments
Paper.paper_summary: This mechanistic murine study demonstrates that Helicobacter hepaticus, acting as a gut pathobiont, is normally tolerated through induction of c-Maf-dependent RORγt+Foxp3+ induced regulatory T cells (iTreg) that suppress pathobiont-specific TH17 responses in the large intestine. In disease-susceptible hosts with impaired IL-10 signaling or c-Maf-deficient iTreg, H. hepaticus instead drives colitogenic TH17 expansion and histopathologically confirmed colitis. The findings establish dysregulated T cell tolerance to pathobionts as a mechanistic hallmark of IBD, supported exclusively by murine experimental models.

Paper.title: The microbiome and human cancer
Paper.authors: Sepich-Poore GD, Zitvogel L, Straussman R, Hasty J, Wargo JA, Knight R
Paper.study_design: Narrative review / critical perspective — no primary data; synthesizes established literature on microbiome-cancer relationships
Paper.population: Not applicable (review article; references human and animal studies from published literature)
Paper.paper_summary: Sepich-Poore et al. provide a comprehensive review of microbial contributions to cancer, describing causal agents, complicit commensals, and therapeutic microbes. Helicobacter pylori is discussed as one of ~11 IACR-designated oncomicrobes, causing gastric cancer and MALT lymphoma via CagA-mediated inflammation, with antibiotic-based therapy (triple/quadruple regimens) as FDA-approved standard of care for H. pylori-associated MALT lymphoma. All associations described in this staging file reflect established literature cited in the review, not primary data from this paper.

Paper.title: First bloodstream infection caused by Prevotella copri in a heart failure elderly patient with Prevotella-dominated gut microbiota: a case report
Paper.authors: Posteraro P, De Maio F, Menchinelli G, Palucci I, Errico FM, Carbone M, Sanguinetti M, Gasbarrini A, Posteraro B
Paper.population: Single 90-year-old male with heart failure (dilated cardiomyopathy) and acute cardiac decompensation; gut microbiota characterised by 16S rRNA sequencing (V3/V4/V6 regions)
Paper.paper_summary: First reported case of clinically significant bloodstream infection caused by Prevotella copri in a heart failure patient. Blood cultures confirmed P. copri bacteremia; concurrent 16S rRNA profiling showed Prevotella genus domination (15.2%) with P. copri at 6.1% relative abundance, supporting gut-to-blood translocation. Patient recovered with metronidazole. Authors explicitly characterize P. copri as a pathobiont.

ClinicalAssociation.association_text: Enterobacteriaceae relative abundance was elevated approximately 10-fold in critically ill ICU patients compared to healthy controls during the first week of ICU admission, as measured by 16S rRNA sequencing of rectal swabs in a prospective cohort of 51 patients, representing the dominant compositional shift in ICU-associated gut dysbiosis.

Progressive Enterobacteriaceae enrichment (≥2-fold increase between consecutive ICU time points) was independently associated with significantly increased odds of nosocomial infection (OR 6.8, 95% CI 1.7–25.3, p=0.01) compared to ICU patients without progressive enrichment, in a prospective cohort of 51 critically ill adults.

Enterobacteriaceae relative abundance positively correlated with systemic inflammatory mediators (IL-8, IL-15, TNF-α, MIP-1α, IL-10) and immature neutrophils in ICU patients, indicating coupling of gut Enterobacteriaceae expansion to innate immune dysregulation during critical illness.

Enterococcaceae was one of two dominant pathobiont families that significantly expanded in the gut microbiota of critically ill ICU patients compared to healthy controls (p=0.0334), representing a key feature of ICU-associated dysbiosis in a prospective cohort of 51 patients.

Enterococcaceae gut bloom in an ICU patient was associated with a nosocomial urinary tract infection caused by Enterococcus faecalis that progressed to secondary bloodstream infection, representing a direct clinical consequence of gut Enterococcaceae expansion documented in a single case within a 51-patient prospective cohort.

ClinicalAssociation.association_text: Ruminococcaceae relative abundance was significantly reduced in critically ill ICU patients compared to healthy controls (ANCOM-II p-adj<0.1), representing a key anaerobic fermenter family lost during critical illness-associated gut dysbiosis in a prospective cohort of 51 patients.

Ruminococcaceae depletion preceded Enterobacteriaceae expansion in critically ill ICU patients, consistent with its role in colonization resistance against pathobiont expansion during critical illness-associated gut dysbiosis.

In an independent newly recruited cohort of 132 anti-PD-1–treated metastatic melanoma patients (n=87 responders, n=45 non-responders), Ruminococcaceae relative abundance was significantly higher in responders versus non-responders (p=0.036 by Wilcoxon rank sum test), replicating the response-associated enrichment pattern identified in a prior cohort.

Across an expanded cohort of 293 metastatic melanoma patients treated with anti-PD-1 or other systemic therapies, Ruminococcaceae was the most significantly enriched taxon in gut microbiota of responders versus non-responders (FDR q<0.1 by Wilcoxon rank sum test), with enrichment persisting after multivariable adjustment for age, sex, BMI, prior treatment, and antibiotic use.

Ruminococcaceae family is depleted in both Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis patients compared to healthy controls across multiple human cohort studies, contributing to the overall pattern of Firmicutes reduction and Bacteroidetes/Firmicutes imbalance that characterizes IBD-associated dysbiosis.

In a phase 1 FMT trial (n=10 anti-PD-1-refractory metastatic melanoma patients), FMT Donor 2 (a melanoma complete responder) was characterized by high Ruminococcaceae relative abundance in stool microbiota; the paper explicitly characterizes this as a previously reported 'immunotherapy-favorable feature' associated with anti-PD-1 response, though Donor 2 recipients produced no clinical responses in this trial.

Ruminococcaceae relative abundance was significantly higher in anti-PD-1 responders versus non-responders in a prospective cohort of 43 metastatic melanoma patients (30R, 13NR; p<0.01 by LEfSe and FDR-adjusted pairwise comparisons), establishing the original human evidence for Ruminococcaceae enrichment as a gut microbiome marker of immunotherapy response.

Lachnospiraceae relative abundance was significantly depleted in critically ill ICU patients compared to healthy controls (ANCOM-II p-adj<0.1), contributing to the loss of colonization resistance and gut dysbiosis during critical illness in a prospective cohort of 51 patients.

Penalized ridge regression identified Lachnospiraceae as one of the most important families negatively associated with progressive Enterobacteriaceae enrichment between ICU days 1 and 3, consistent with a colonization resistance role against pathobiont expansion during critical illness.

In a phase 1 FMT trial (n=10 anti-PD-1-refractory metastatic melanoma patients), both FMT donors who had achieved complete response to anti-PD-1 therapy were characterized by high Lachnospiraceae relative abundance in their stool microbiota; the paper explicitly characterizes this as a previously reported 'immunotherapy-favorable feature' of the gut microbiome associated with response to anti-PD-1 therapy.

In a murine CDI model, susceptibility to C. difficile colonization following antibiotic treatment was associated with loss of the normal cecal microbial community (mainly Lachnospiraceae) and a relative increase in Enterobacteriaceae; disease severity was related to the recovery dynamics of these families, with more severe outcomes in mice where Lachnospiraceae failed to return post-antibiotic and Enterobacteriaceae continued to dominate.

ClinicalAssociation.association_text: Clostridioides difficile was identified as the causative pathogen of diarrhea/colitis in one critically ill ICU patient (Patient 43) who had concurrent progressive fecal Enterobacteriaceae enrichment, representing an incidental CDI case within a 51-patient prospective cohort studying ICU-associated gut dysbiosis.
Children with IBD have an approximately eleven-fold higher likelihood of developing CDI compared to non-IBD peers, with one state-level dataset reporting an incidence rate ratio of 12.7.
CDI prevalence in pediatric IBD ranges from 3.5% to 69% depending on the population studied, reflecting both true infection and high rates of asymptomatic colonization.
Between 10% and 25% of children with IBD carry toxigenic C. difficile asymptomatically, which substantially complicates interpretation of positive diagnostic tests.
CDI in children with IBD is associated with prolonged hospitalization, with average length of stay increasing from 6 to 8 days compared to IBD patients without CDI.
Children with IBD and CDI have an 8% rate of abdominal surgery within 6 months compared to 3% in IBD patients without CDI (p<0.01).
CDI in pediatric IBD is associated with recurrence rates of 25% to 34%, defined as a new episode within 8 weeks of the initial infection.
Approximately 3% to 7% of children with CDI progress to fulminant disease presenting as hypotension, shock, ileus, or toxic megacolon.
CDI accounts for 0.3% of all pediatric colectomies, and 74.8% of those colectomies occurred in IBD patients, indicating that the IBD-CDI comorbidity disproportionately drives surgical outcomes.
67% of 111 pediatric IBD patients with CDI required escalation of immunosuppressive therapy, including addition of an immunomodulator or biologic agent, during or after CDI treatment.
Children with IBD and CDI are more likely to require systemic steroids or TNF inhibitors in the future compared to IBD patients without CDI.

In pediatric IBD, clindamycin and third-generation cephalosporins carry the highest risk for CDI, while broad-spectrum penicillins, fluoroquinolones, and carbapenems pose moderate risk; tetracyclines and aminoglycosides are rarely associated with CDI.

5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA) therapy is associated with increased CDI risk in pediatric IBD (odds ratio 1.95, 95% CI 1.26-3.0), while steroids, immunomodulators, and biologic agents show no significant association in a meta-analysis of 14 studies.

Children with IBD and CDI exhibit depletion of butyrate-producing Firmicutes and expansion of opportunistic Proteobacteria, with altered bile acid profiles showing elevated primary bile acids (promoting C. difficile spore germination) and depleted secondary bile acids (which inhibit C. difficile growth).
Multi-omic analysis revealed distinct metabolic profiles in pediatric IBD patients with CDI versus without CDI, including elevated taurine and isocaproyltaurine in CDI-positive samples.

Higher prevalence of toxigenic C. difficile is observed in newly diagnosed pediatric and adult IBD patients even in the absence of prior antibiotic exposure, suggesting that colonization may precede or contribute to IBD onset, though C. difficile is not considered a primary cause of IBD.
In pediatric IBD, acid-suppressing medications (PPIs and H2RAs) show no significant association with CDI risk, in contrast to their known risk association in the general pediatric population.

FMT achieves comparable efficacy for recurrent CDI in IBD children versus non-IBD children (76% vs. 81%, p=0.17), with success more likely when using fresh donor stool, in the absence of active diarrhea at time of procedure, and with a shorter interval between CDI diagnosis and FMT.

CDI in pediatric IBD is more frequently and severely observed in patients with active or severe IBD; CDI is more common in ulcerative colitis than Crohn's disease in adults, though pediatric studies show more variable findings.
CDI in children is more frequently community-acquired than in adults, with approximately three-quarters of all pediatric CDI cases occurring in community rather than healthcare settings.

Approximately 30% of patients with CDI develop recurrence, most within the first 8 weeks following symptom resolution; approximately 50% of those with a first recurrence go on to develop multiple recurrent infections.

Recurrent CDI is associated with a 33% increase in all-cause mortality, a 2.5-fold increase in hospital admission rate, 4-fold longer hospital stay, and significantly higher total costs compared with the initial CDI episode (mean £31,121 vs £12,710; P<0.002).
Cumulative antibiotic exposure is the dominant risk factor for CDI; each additional day of antibiotic exposure increases the odds of CDI by 12.8% (OR 1.128; P<0.0001).

CDI incidence in England increased by approximately 25% in 2021-2023 relative to pre-pandemic levels following the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic; similar post-pandemic CDI increases were also reported in Canada, Greece, Spain, and Australia.

RBX2660 (Rebyota), an FDA-approved standardised microbiota-based enema biotherapeutic, achieved a modelled treatment success (absence of CDI diarrhoea at 8 weeks) of 70.6% vs 57.5% for placebo (absolute improvement 13.1%, 95%CI 2.3-24.0) in a Phase III double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial for prevention of recurrent CDI.

SER-109 (Vowst), an FDA-approved oral Firmicutes spore-based biotherapeutic, prevented CDI recurrence in 88% vs 60% of placebo recipients at 8 weeks (RR 0.32, 95%CI 0.18-0.58; P<0.001), with benefit sustained at 24 weeks (79% vs 53%), in a Phase III multicentre, randomised, placebo-controlled trial.
Older age, chronic kidney disease, and recent hospitalisation were identified as independent risk factors for multiple CDI recurrences in a 2024 cohort study summarised in this review.

VE303, a defined bacterial consortium of 8 distinct Clostridial species, reduced rCDI recurrence to 13.8% in the high-dose group (10 capsules daily, n=29) versus 45.5% in the placebo group (n=22) at 8 weeks in the phase 2 CONSORTIUM randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial enrolling adults with prior CDI history or study-defined high recurrence risk.

RBX7455, an oral lyophilized LBP derived from RBX2660, achieved rCDI recurrence rates of 10% (4 capsules twice daily for 4 days, n=10) and 0% (2 capsules twice daily for 2 days, n=10) at 8 weeks in a phase 1 dose-ranging open-label trial; no recurrences were observed in any group between 8 weeks and 6 months.

Secondary bile acids, produced by commensal gut bacteria from primary bile acids, inhibit C. difficile spore germination and reduce virulence; antibiotic-induced dysbiosis significantly depletes these protective metabolites, and secondary bile acids are markedly reduced in patients with initial and recurrent CDI compared to pre-CDI baseline, thereby facilitating C. difficile spore germination and proliferation.

rCDI occurs in up to 35% of patients after their first CDI episode; following a first recurrence, 45–65% of patients experience at least one additional recurrence; rCDI affects nearly half a million Americans annually and accounts for up to USD 4.8 billion in excessive acute care costs in the US.
European CDC estimates overall CDI mortality at 4.1%, while hospitalized patients face mortality rates up to 28%.
Over 35% of patients treated for initial CDI experience recurrent CDI, and approximately 65% of those with initial rCDI undergo subsequent recurrences.
Approximately 50% of patients experiencing a second CDI episode progress to three or more recurrences, with up to 43% of those patients facing elevated sepsis risk.
Per-patient annual rCDI-attributable direct medical costs in the USA range from USD 67,837 to USD 82,268.
Bezlotoxumab reduced rCDI recurrence rate to 15.8% versus 28.9% for standard-of-care, with a relative risk of 0.57 (95% CI: 0.45-0.72).
FMT achieves 80-90% efficacy in preventing rCDI, with colonoscopy achieving a 94.8% cure rate and oral capsules 92.1%, significantly outperforming vancomycin alone (31% success).
FMT has an NNT of 2 for rCDI prevention, compared to NNT 4 for SER-109, NNT 8 for RBX2660, and NNT 10 for bezlotoxumab.
Patients with renal insufficiency, ongoing antibiotic treatment, oncological diseases, or immunodeficiencies face higher rCDI risk, with high-risk patient groups showing rCDI rates up to 50%.

In the phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled PUNCH CD3 trial (n=267; 180 Rebyota:87 placebo), a single rectal dose of Rebyota (fecal microbiota, live-jslm; RBX2660) following antibiotic therapy for rCDI reduced recurrence to 29.6% versus 41.9% in the placebo group (estimated 12.3% absolute difference; posterior probability of superiority 0.986, exceeding the FDA-specified threshold of 0.975), with 90% sustained clinical response at 6 months; Rebyota received FDA approval on 30 November 2022 as the first live biotherapeutic product for prevention of rCDI.

In the phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled ECOSPOR III trial (n=182; 89 Vowst:93 placebo), a 3-day oral course of Vowst (fecal microbiota spores, live-brpk; SER-109) following antibiotic therapy for rCDI reduced recurrence to 12% versus 40% in the placebo group at 8 weeks (RR 0.32, 95% CI 0.18–0.58, p<0.001), with 88% sustained response at 24 weeks; Vowst received FDA approval on 26 April 2023 as the first oral live biotherapeutic product for prevention of rCDI.

In the phase 2, double-blind, placebo-controlled PRISM3 trial (n=198; 102 CP101:96 placebo), a single oral dose of CP101 following antibiotic therapy for rCDI achieved 74.5% non-recurrence versus 61.5% in placebo (p<0.05; 33.8% relative risk reduction) at 8 weeks; the subsequent phase 3 trial (PRISM4) was terminated in January 2023 due to funding challenges and enrollment difficulties.
Clostridioides difficile is the primary cause of nosocomial gastrointestinal infections in industrialized countries, with incidence, morbidity, and mortality increasing over recent decades.
Clostridioides difficile causes pseudomembranous colitis and, when left untreated, can progress to toxic megacolon, a potentially life-threatening complication.
Clostridioides difficile colonization is highly prevalent in infants, while fewer than 5% of adults are asymptomatic carriers.
Antibiotic-induced disruption of the gut microbiome triggers germination of C. difficile spores into vegetative cells that produce enterotoxins, causing watery diarrhea and colonic inflammation.

Clostridioides difficile produces p-cresol via reductive fermentation of tyrosine, which inhibits the motility of competing gut bacteria (including protective commensals) and confers a colonization advantage in the antibiotic-disrupted gut; p-cresol production is described as a virulence-relevant competitive mechanism specific to C. difficile among gut pathogens.

Patients with inflammatory bowel disease have a significantly elevated risk of Clostridioides difficile infection compared to the general population, with IBD-associated dysbiosis — characterized by loss of protective Lachnospiraceae and Bacteroidetes members — creating permissive gut conditions for C. difficile colonization and CDI recurrence.

In antibiotic-treated mice, cecal cholate levels become elevated while bacterial transformation to secondary bile acids (deoxycholate, lithocholate) is greatly suppressed; this antibiotic-induced shift in the bile acid pool promotes C. difficile spore germination by providing the cholate co-stimulant while removing the inhibitory secondary bile acids that are normally produced by commensal microbiota from primary bile acids.

ClinicalAssociation.association_text: Akkermansia muciniphila displays intrinsic resistance to glycopeptide antibiotics, indicating that antimicrobial resistance profiles of novel probiotic organisms may have clinical implications for gut microbiota management in susceptible patient populations.

Akkermansia muciniphila abundance is reduced in Porphyromonas gingivalis OMV-induced gut dysbiosis in murine models, alongside reductions in Firmicutes and Lactobacillus spp., accompanied by systemic inflammation and insulin resistance.

Akkermansia muciniphila abundance is inversely associated with type 2 diabetes mellitus; its depletion is linked to impaired gut barrier function, increased intestinal permeability, and systemic metabolic dysfunction.

Akkermansia muciniphila is protective against periodontitis; its abundance is inversely associated with periodontal disease severity, suggesting a gut–oral axis role for this commensal in modulating oral inflammation.

Akkermansia muciniphila ameliorates experimental colitis in murine models by reinforcing gut epithelial barrier integrity, reducing mucosal permeability, and attenuating intestinal inflammatory responses.

Akkermansia muciniphila enhances antitumor immunity in colorectal cancer patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy; higher pre-treatment Am abundance correlates with improved immunotherapy response.
Akkermansia muciniphila is associated with enhanced antitumor immunity in prostate cancer; its abundance supports immune checkpoint inhibitor efficacy in preclinical and observational contexts.

Akkermansia muciniphila protects intestinal epithelial barrier integrity by degrading the mucin layer in a regulated manner, reducing gut permeability and limiting translocation of microbial products that drive systemic inflammation.

Akkermansia muciniphila was among organisms enriched in responders (objective response or stable disease >12 months) to FMT plus pembrolizumab in a Phase 2 trial of 15 PD-1-refractory advanced melanoma patients; transkingdom network analysis identified it as negatively correlated with circulating CXCL8 (IL-8), an immunosuppressive cytokine elevated in non-responders and associated with immune checkpoint blockade resistance.

Akkermansia muciniphila is consistently depleted in both Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis patients compared to healthy controls in multiple human cohort studies; its depletion correlates with increased gut permeability and mucosal inflammation, and the review identifies loss of A. muciniphila as a contributing factor to impaired gut barrier integrity in IBD.

Akkermansia muciniphila was enriched in the gut microbiome of non-responders to cancer therapeutics (immune checkpoint blockade, platinum-based chemotherapy, EGFR TKI) compared with responders among patients with advanced NSCLC (stage IIIB/IV), identified by LEfSe analysis of 16S rRNA gut metagenomics; the authors note that immunomodulatory effects of gut microbiota on cancer therapy may differ by cancer type, race, and geography.

Higher pre-treatment stool abundance of A. muciniphila was significantly associated with clinical response and longer progression-free survival in NSCLC and RCC patients receiving PD-1/PD-L1 blockade; A. muciniphila was detectable in 69% (11/16) of partial responders vs. 34% (15/44) of progressors (P=0.007) in the discovery metagenomics cohort (n=100), with findings replicated in two independent validation cohorts (n=53 NSCLC+RCC and n=239 NSCLC).

Antibiotic use (β-lactams, fluoroquinolones, or macrolides) within 2 months before or 1 month after initiation of PD-1/PD-L1 mAb was independently associated with significantly shorter progression-free survival and overall survival in 249 patients with NSCLC, RCC, and urothelial carcinoma (median OS: 15.3 vs. 8.3 months; P<0.001), confirmed in 239 additional NSCLC patients, implicating antibiotic-mediated gut dysbiosis — including depletion of A. muciniphila — as a driver of primary ICI resistance.

Fecal microbiota transplantation from ICI-responding NSCLC/RCC patients into germ-free or antibiotic-treated mice conferred sensitivity to PD-1 blockade, increasing CXCR3+CD4+ tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes and PD-L1 expression on splenic T cells; FMT from non-responders conveyed resistance to PD-1 blockade, establishing a causal role for gut microbiome composition — including A. muciniphila — in determining ICI efficacy.

Oral supplementation with A. muciniphila in antibiotic-dysbiotic mice restored PD-1 blockade antitumor efficacy against RET melanoma, MCA-205 sarcoma, and orthotopic LLC lung cancers in an IL-12-dependent manner, increasing CCR9+CXCR3+CD4+ central memory T cell recruitment into mesenteric lymph nodes and tumor beds, and elevating intratumoral CD4+/FoxP3+ ratios.

Aspergillus terreus was isolated from bronchoalveolar lavage in a post-allogeneic HSCT patient with B-cell ALL, causing invasive pulmonary aspergillosis that required combination antifungal therapy with isavuconazole and caspofungin.

ClinicalAssociation.association_text: Bifidobacterium species display intrinsic vancomycin resistance but lack acquired resistance genes (vanA, vanB, vanC) and have fewer reported associations with bloodstream infections compared to Lacticaseibacillus spp., suggesting a relatively lower BSI risk profile for immunocompromised patients receiving Bifidobacterium-containing probiotics.

Clostridium scindens directly inhibits Clostridioides difficile colonisation in the gut via 7α-dehydroxylation of primary bile acids to secondary bile acids (deoxycholic acid, lithocholic acid), which suppress C. difficile spore germination and vegetative cell outgrowth; this mechanism was demonstrated in a gnotobiotic mouse model and is reviewed as foundational evidence for precision microbiome reconstitution against CDI.
ClinicalAssociation.evidence_type: narrative review (primary evidence: gnotobiotic mouse model)

ClinicalAssociation.association_text: Clostridium scindens is identified in this review as a candidate species for precision microbiome reconstitution therapies to restore gut colonisation resistance and prevent C. difficile proliferation following antibiotic-induced dysbiosis.

Enterococcus faecalis was isolated from a wound swab in a post-HSCT immunocompromised patient with B-cell ALL; treatment with cefepime was initiated but discontinued due to cefepime-induced neurotoxicity.

GF C57BL/6 mice monocolonized with E. faecalis (n=6–10) showed translocation to mesenteric veins, MLNs, and liver but did NOT develop gut barrier leakage (FITC-dextran not elevated), anti-RNA IgG, or anti-dsDNA IgG autoantibodies at 8 weeks post-colonization, in contrast to E. gallinarum-monocolonized mice; Th17 cells were not expanded in small intestinal lamina propria or MLNs (n=5 per group).

E. faecalis lysate or RNA induced significantly lower expression of ERV gp70, β2-glycoprotein I, type I IFN-α, and AhR/CYP1A1 in murine and human hepatocytes compared to E. gallinarum (ANOVA, p<0.05 to p<0.0001, n=3 each); serum anti-E. faecalis RNA IgG was not elevated in SLE (n=15) or AIH (n=17) patients relative to healthy controls (n=9), distinguishing it from E. gallinarum.

ClinicalAssociation.association_text: Fusobacterium nucleatum acts as a bridging colonizer in periodontal biofilm and contributes to the progression of periodontitis through immune dysregulation and polymicrobial community assembly at the periodontal niche.

Fusobacterium nucleatum OMVs deliver FadA adhesin to colorectal epithelial cells, activating Wnt/β-catenin signaling and promoting tumor invasion, immune evasion, and chemotherapy resistance in colorectal cancer.

Fusobacterium nucleatum is enriched in the gut mucosa of patients with inflammatory bowel disease, and its OMVs exacerbate mucosal inflammation and intestinal barrier disruption in murine models of ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease.
Fusobacterium nucleatum is associated with rheumatoid arthritis pathogenesis; Fn OMVs activate pro-inflammatory TLR-mediated pathways relevant to synovial inflammation.
Fusobacterium nucleatum OMVs induce acute hepatotoxicity and liver injury in murine models via the gut–liver axis, involving TLR4-dependent signaling and NLRP3 inflammasome activation in hepatocytes.

Fusobacterium nucleatum has been detected in human atherosclerotic plaques and promotes platelet aggregation and systemic pro-inflammatory signaling, suggesting a potential role in atherosclerosis pathogenesis.
Fusobacterium nucleatum is associated with lung cancer; Fn OMVs may facilitate pulmonary immune evasion and metastatic seeding via systemic dissemination from the oral-gut axis.
Fusobacterium nucleatum has been detected in breast cancer tissue and is associated with tumor progression and immune evasion in breast cancer patients.
Fusobacterium nucleatum induces gut microbiota dysbiosis characterized by loss of protective commensals and intestinal barrier disruption, contributing to systemic inflammatory burden.

ClinicalAssociation.association_text: Gut intestinal domination by Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus (71.6% relative abundance by shotgun metagenomics) was temporally associated with bloodstream infection in a post-allogeneic HSCT patient with B-cell ALL; genomic comparison between the gut-dominant strain and the blood culture isolate revealed only 18 SNP differences, supporting direct gut-to-bloodstream translocation as the mechanism of bacteremia.

Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus was isolated from multiple concurrent blood culture sites (PICC, CVC, peripheral vein) in a severely immunocompromised post-HSCT patient during the final week of life, with markedly elevated sepsis markers (procalcitonin 2.4 ± 1.87 ng/L; D-dimer 7518 ± 2801.7 ng/mL), contributing to a fatal multi-organ toxicity outcome.

Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus demonstrates intrinsic resistance to glycopeptides (teicoplanin and vancomycin) with no established EUCAST breakpoints, complicating antimicrobial management of Lactobacillus bloodstream infections in immunocompromised patients.

Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG)–based probiotic administration to germ-free mice colonized with an ICB complete responder's microbiota significantly impaired antitumor response to anti-PD-L1 therapy, resulting in significantly larger tumors compared to sterile water control (P=0.01 by likelihood ratio test in linear mixed model; n=4–5 per group), with concomitant reduction in gut microbiome alpha diversity (inverse Simpson index, P=0.38 vs. control — non-significant trend).

LGG-based probiotic administration significantly reduced the frequency of IFN-γ–positive CD8+ cytotoxic T cells in the tumor microenvironment of anti-PD-L1–treated melanoma-bearing germ-free mice (P=0.03 by supervised flow cytometry analysis; n=6 per group), indicating suppression of intratumoral cytotoxic T cell responses as a mechanism of impaired ICB efficacy.

Pediococcus acidilactici was the second most abundant species in the gut microbiome (17.4% by shotgun metagenomics) at the time of Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus bloodstream infection in a post-HSCT patient with B-cell ALL, co-dominating a markedly dysbiotic Bacillota-predominant microbiome (98.5% Bacillota total).

ClinicalAssociation.association_text: Porphyromonas gingivalis acts as a keystone pathobiont in periodontitis, orchestrating immune dysregulation and promoting polymicrobial community virulence in the periodontal niche.

Porphyromonas gingivalis is associated with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) pathogenesis via PPAD-mediated citrullination of host proteins; anti-PPAD and anti-RgpA antibodies demonstrate positive predictive values of 82.5% and 93.7% for RA diagnosis, respectively.

Porphyromonas gingivalis OMVs are associated with Alzheimer's disease-like pathology in mice, inducing neuroinflammation via microglial NLRP3 inflammasome activation, tau phosphorylation, and cognitive impairment following oral administration.
Porphyromonas gingivalis is associated with type 1 diabetes mellitus.

Porphyromonas gingivalis and its OMVs are associated with cardiovascular disease risk, including platelet aggregation and potential contribution to atherosclerosis and myocardial infarction via systemic inflammation.

Porphyromonas gingivalis is associated with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) progression, inducing gut dysbiosis with reduced SCFA producers, gingipain-mediated ferroptosis in hepatocytes, and elevated hepatic lipid accumulation and glucose intolerance in murine models.
Porphyromonas gingivalis is associated with colorectal cancer.
Porphyromonas gingivalis is associated with esophageal cancer.
Porphyromonas gingivalis is associated with pancreatic cancer.
Porphyromonas gingivalis is associated with hepatocellular carcinoma.
Porphyromonas gingivalis OMVs exacerbate diabetic retinopathy, increasing blood-retinal barrier permeability and pathological microvasculature alterations in a streptozotocin-induced mouse model.

Porphyromonas gingivalis induces gut microbiota dysbiosis characterized by reduced Firmicutes, Lactobacillus spp., and Akkermansia muciniphila and increased Bacteroidales, accompanied by systemic inflammation and insulin resistance.
Porphyromonas gingivalis OMVs disrupt trophoblast interactions with vascular and immune cells in an in vitro early placentation model, suggesting a potential contribution to pregnancy complications.

Staphylococcus epidermidis caused a catheter-related bloodstream infection during conditioning chemotherapy in a 20-year-old immunocompromised patient undergoing allogeneic HSCT for B-cell ALL, treated empirically with meropenem, vancomycin, and liposomal amphotericin B.

A multidrug-resistant S. epidermidis clone (ST5R, cfr on plasmid pMB151a, also resistant to methicillin, levofloxacin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and gentamicin) caused 31 of 39 (79%) linezolid-resistant bloodstream infections in leukemia patients at a major cancer center; prior linezolid use in the preceding 90 days was significantly more common in patients with linezolid-resistant vs linezolid-susceptible ST5 infections (79% vs 19%; P<0.001), and cumulative linezolid exposure was significantly higher (median 12 vs 0 days; P<0.001), indicating that both nosocomial clonal transmission and antibiotic selection pressure drove invasive multidrug-resistant S. epidermidis emergence.

Bifidobacterium longum was among bacterial species enriched in responders (objective response or stable disease >12 months) to FMT plus pembrolizumab in a Phase 2 trial of 15 PD-1-refractory advanced melanoma patients (NCT03341143), confirming its previously reported association with favorable anti-PD-1 response in human melanoma.

Bifidobacterium longum was among 8 commensal species significantly enriched in pre-treatment stool of metastatic melanoma anti-PD-1 responders (n=16) versus non-responders (n=26) by integrated 16S rRNA, shotgun metagenomic, and qPCR analysis (P<0.05, permutation test); fecal microbiota from responding patients conveyed improved tumor control and augmented CD8+ T cell infiltration in germ-free mouse recipients.

Enterococcus gallinarum undergoes within-host evolution into mucosally-adapted lineages that exhibit significantly increased translocation to the mesenteric lymph nodes and liver compared to luminal lineages in germ-free monocolonised mice.

Enterococcus gallinarum mucosally-adapted liver isolates exhibit significantly increased resistance to lysozyme-mediated growth inhibition, cathelicidin-related antimicrobial peptide (mCRAMP) killing, and macrophage phagocytosis compared to luminal faecal isolates in vitro.

Enterococcus gallinarum liver-adapted isolates induce increased intestinal permeability and reduced epithelial barrier defences, including decreased mucus production, reduced intraepithelial lymphocyte recruitment, and altered tight junction protein expression, in germ-free monocolonised mice.

Enterococcus gallinarum liver-adapted isolates induce increased hepatic inflammatory gene expression, including upregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines, interferon-stimulated genes, serum amyloid A proteins, and collagen, compared to faecal isolates in germ-free monocolonised mice.

Enterococcus gallinarum translocation to the liver exacerbates lupus-like autoimmune manifestations including hepatosplenomegaly, proteinuria, and elevated anti-dsDNA autoantibodies in a TLR7 agonist (imiquimod)-induced autoimmunity mouse model.

Enterococcus gallinarum mucosally-adapted isolates produce an enhanced capsular polysaccharide layer that facilitates evasion of innate immune recognition and is associated with increased liver translocation in germ-free monocolonised mice.

Enterococcus gallinarum has been detected in liver biopsies from patients with autoimmune hepatitis and primary sclerosing cholangitis, as reported in prior studies cited by the authors; this finding motivated the in vivo translocation experiments in this paper.

E. gallinarum was detected by species-specific PCR and immunostaining in liver biopsies of 3/3 tested SLE patients and 5/6 tested AIH patients but in 0/6 healthy cadaveric liver donor controls; 16S rDNA sequencing showed Enterococcus spp. predominance in AIH and cirrhosis liver tissues relative to healthy controls (human case-control).

Serum IgG antibody titers against E. gallinarum whole bacteria and its RNA were significantly elevated in the majority of SLE (n=15) and AIH (n=17) patients versus healthy controls (n=9); anti-E. gallinarum RNA IgG correlated with anti-human RNA autoantibody titers in SLE (R²=0.5132, p=0.0027) and AIH (R²=0.8245, p<0.0001) patients (human case-control).

Monocolonization of germ-free C57BL/6 mice with E. gallinarum (n=4–10) induced gut barrier leakage, translocation to mesenteric veins, MLNs, and liver, and elevated anti-RNA IgG and anti-dsDNA IgG autoantibodies at 8 weeks (p<0.05 to p<0.001 vs. GF); neither E. faecalis nor B. thetaiotaomicron monocolonization induced autoantibodies under the same conditions.

E. gallinarum monocolonization of GF C57BL/6 mice induced marked Th17 expansion in the small intestinal lamina propria (20.1% IL-17A+ vs. 0.50% GF, p<0.0001) and mesenteric lymph nodes (15.1% vs. 0.035%, p<0.001); Th17 expansion was absent in E. faecalis- and B. thetaiotaomicron-monocolonized mice (n=5 per group).

E. gallinarum lysate or RNA co-cultured with autoimmune-prone (NZW×BXSB)F1 hepatocytes induced expression of autoantigens ERV gp70 (~15-fold) and β2-glycoprotein I (~3-fold), type I IFN-α (~30-fold), and the AhR/CYP1A1 pathway significantly above induction by E. faecalis or B. thetaiotaomicron (ANOVA, p<0.05 to p<0.0001, n=3 each); the same pattern was replicated in primary human hepatocytes.

Administration of the AhR antagonist CH223191 to autoimmune-prone (NZW×BXSB)F1 mice gavaged with E. gallinarum significantly reduced serum anti-RNA IgG (p<0.001) and anti-dsDNA IgG (p<0.001) vs. untreated E. gallinarum-gavaged mice (n=4 per group), confirming that the AhR pathway mediates E. gallinarum-driven autoantibody induction.

Oral vancomycin or ampicillin treatment of autoimmune-prone (NZW×BXSB)F1 mice (n=15 per group) prevented mortality, suppressed E. gallinarum translocation to mesenteric veins, MLNs, and liver, and eliminated anti-dsDNA IgG, anti-RNA IgG, anti-β2GPI IgG autoantibodies and Th17/Tfh cell expansion vs. untreated controls (p<0.05 to p<0.0001); neomycin was less effective and metronidazole had no significant effect on survival.

Intramuscular vaccination with heat-killed E. gallinarum in autoimmune-prone (NZW×BXSB)F1 mice reduced serum autoantibody levels, prolonged survival, and prevented translocation to internal organs; vaccination against E. faecalis or B. thetaiotaomicron had no protective effect, indicating specificity of the E. gallinarum-driven autoimmune response.

ClinicalAssociation.association_text: Faecalibacterium prausnitzii relative abundance was enriched in anti-PD-1 responders versus non-responders in the shotgun metagenomic subset of 111 metastatic melanoma patients (n=71 responders, n=40 non-responders; fig. S2A), providing species-level confirmation of its association with immunotherapy response.

Faecalibacterium prausnitzii was significantly enriched in anti-PD-1 responders versus non-responders in metagenomic WGS of fecal samples from 25 metastatic melanoma patients (14R, 11NR), establishing the original species-level human evidence of its enrichment in the gut microbiome of immunotherapy responders (Fig. 2F).

Faecalibacterium prausnitzii was among the bacterial species significantly enriched in responders (objective response or stable disease >12 months) to FMT plus pembrolizumab in a Phase 2 trial of 15 PD-1-refractory advanced melanoma patients, confirming prior reports; transkingdom network analysis further identified it as negatively correlated with circulating CXCL8 (IL-8), an immunosuppressive cytokine elevated in non-responders.

Antibiotic-induced depletion of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii in one PD-1-refractory melanoma patient undergoing FMT plus pembrolizumab (PT-18-0018) was associated with pronounced disruption of the transplanted microbiome and clinical disease progression; re-transplantation from the same donor restored gut colonization and was followed by renewed disease stabilization.

Low Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance at the time of ileocolonic resection is an independent predictor of postoperative endoscopic recurrence in Crohn's disease patients; this finding, from human prospective cohort data synthesized in this review, establishes F. prausnitzii as a prognostic biomarker for CD surgical outcomes.

Faecalibacterium prausnitzii exerts direct anti-inflammatory effects in the gut via inhibition of the NF-κB signaling pathway; this mechanism, demonstrated in cell-based and animal models and cited in the context of IBD, underlies its role as a protective commensal whose depletion contributes to sustained intestinal inflammation in Crohn's disease.

ClinicalAssociation.association_text: Faecalibacterium genus relative abundance was significantly higher in anti-PD-1 responders versus non-responders in a newly recruited independent cohort of 132 metastatic melanoma patients (n=87 responders, n=45 non-responders; p=0.018 by Wilcoxon rank sum test), supporting its role as a gut microbiota marker of immunotherapy response.

In melanoma patients treated with ICB (n=123), Faecalibacterium genus abundance was numerically higher in patients reporting sufficient dietary fiber intake (≥20 g/day) and no probiotic use — the subgroup with significantly longer progression-free survival (median PFS not reached versus 13 months, P=0.015 vs. all other groups) — though the Faecalibacterium difference per se did not reach statistical significance due to small group size (n=22 in optimal group).

Faecalibacterium genus is significantly and consistently depleted in Crohn's disease patients compared to healthy controls across multiple human cohort studies, with the degree of depletion correlating with disease activity; this depletion is identified in this review as one of the most reproducible microbial signatures of IBD-associated dysbiosis.

Faecalibacterium genus was significantly enriched in anti-PD-1 responders versus non-responders in the gut microbiome of 43 metastatic melanoma patients (30R, 13NR; FDR-adjusted pairwise comparisons and LEfSe; p<0.01), establishing the original human evidence for genus-level enrichment as a marker of immunotherapy response.

High Faecalibacterium abundance (above median) was associated with significantly prolonged progression-free survival compared to low abundance in 39 anti-PD-1-treated metastatic melanoma patients (p=0.03; multivariate Cox HR=2.95, 95% CI 1.31–7.29), identifying it as an independent gut microbiome predictor of immunotherapy outcome.

Faecalibacterium genus abundance was significantly positively correlated with CD8+ T cell density in pre-treatment tumors of melanoma patients on anti-PD-1 therapy (r²=0.42, p<0.01; n=15 matched tumor-microbiome samples), linking gut microbiome composition to intratumoral anti-tumor immunity.

Limosilactobacillus reuteri exhibited liver translocation in a subset of germ-free mice following three-month monocolonization, demonstrating capacity for bacterial translocation from gut to liver in an animal model.

Limosilactobacillus reuteri exhibits divergent within-host evolution with mucosal and luminal lineage diversification and enhanced immune evasion capacity in a germ-free mouse monocolonization model, with a pattern broadly similar to Enterococcus gallinarum.

Limosilactobacillus reuteri liver-adapted isolates demonstrate enhanced liver persistence in vivo, with liver populations enriched for a triple mutant genotype (lacS/greA/ccpA) compared to faecal isolates in germ-free monocolonized mice.
Limosilactobacillus reuteri has been previously reported to translocate to the liver in a mouse model of lupus, as cited in this study as prior evidence motivating its use as a comparative organism.

Bacteroides fragilis exhibits mucosal/luminal lineage divergence (within-host evolution) in germ-free monocolonised mice but did not translocate to the liver, unlike Enterococcus gallinarum, suggesting that within-host evolutionary diversification is a broad property of gut bacteria but that liver translocation capacity is taxon-specific.

ClinicalAssociation.association_text: GF C57BL/6 mice monocolonized with B. thetaiotaomicron (n=6–10) showed no detectable translocation to mesenteric veins, MLNs, or liver (CFU=0 at all extra-intestinal sites), no gut barrier leakage, and no induction of anti-RNA IgG or anti-dsDNA IgG autoantibodies at 8 weeks post-colonization; Th17 cells were not expanded in small intestinal lamina propria or MLNs (n=5 per group), in contrast to E. gallinarum monocolonization.

B. thetaiotaomicron lysate or RNA co-cultured with murine and human hepatocytes did not significantly induce ERV gp70, β2-glycoprotein I, type I IFN-α, or AhR/CYP1A1 expression above medium control (n=3 each); serum anti-B. thetaiotaomicron RNA IgG was not elevated in SLE (n=15) or AIH (n=17) patients versus healthy controls (n=9), confirming immunological quiescence relative to E. gallinarum.

Intramuscular vaccination against B. thetaiotaomicron in autoimmune-prone (NZW×BXSB)F1 mice had no effect on serum autoantibody levels or survival, confirming that B. thetaiotaomicron does not drive autoimmune pathology and that the autoimmune response is specific to E. gallinarum.

Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron was significantly enriched in anti-PD-1 non-responders versus responders by metagenomic WGS in fecal samples from 25 metastatic melanoma patients (14R, 11NR), identifying it as part of a gut microbiome signature associated with immunotherapy non-response (Fig. 2F).

ClinicalAssociation.association_text: B. bifidum was significantly enriched in stool samples of patients with non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) who responded to cancer therapeutics (partial response) compared to non-responders, as determined by 16S rRNA LEfSe analysis and confirmed by quantitative PCR (P=0.0022).

B. bifidum abundance remained significantly higher in NSCLC responders compared to non-responders even after excluding EGFR TKI-treated patients (P=0.0128), supporting a treatment-agnostic association between B. bifidum enrichment and therapeutic response.

Oral administration of B. bifidum strains K57 and K18 in combination with anti-PD-1 antibody significantly reduced tumour burden in syngeneic MC38 colon cancer mouse models compared to anti-PD-1 alone (P<0.0001 for both strains).

Oral administration of B. bifidum strains K57 and K18 in combination with oxaliplatin significantly reduced tumour growth in syngeneic MC38 mouse models compared to oxaliplatin alone (P=0.0004 for K57, P=0.0001 for K18).

B. bifidum K57 combined with anti-PD-1 reduced tumour burden in orthotopic and subcutaneous Lewis lung carcinoma (LLC1) syngeneic mouse models, including in anti-PD-1-resistant settings (P=0.038 for orthotopic model).

B. bifidum K57 combined with anti-PD-1 significantly reduced tumour growth in anti-PD-1-resistant 4T1 breast cancer syngeneic mouse models, whereas anti-PD-1 or B. bifidum K57 alone showed little antitumour effect (P<0.0001).

Synergistic B. bifidum strains K57 and K18 induced significantly more IFN-γ secretion from human CD8+ T cells in autologous monocyte co-culture assays compared to non-synergistic strains; IFN-γ induction was abrogated by TLR2-blocking antibody, implicating peptidoglycan-TLR2 signalling as the mechanism.

In syngeneic mouse tumour models, B. bifidum K57 combined with anti-PD-1 significantly increased intratumoral CD8+ T cell and effector CD8+ T cell populations and CD8+/Treg ratios in tumour and spleen, and elevated IFN-γ and IL-2 while reducing TNF-α and IL-10 expression in tumours.

Functional metagenome profiling (HUMAnN2) of stool WGS from NSCLC patients showed that the peptidoglycan biosynthesis pathway was significantly enriched in responders with B. bifidum compared to non-responders (P=0.012), linking B. bifidum peptidoglycan capacity to therapeutic response.

Serum metabolomics in B. bifidum K57-treated mice showed elevated L-tryptophan levels; in vitro L-tryptophan treatment increased IFN-γ production from activated human CD8+ T cells (P=0.0082), suggesting a tryptophan-mediated immunostimulatory mechanism.

Overall serum lipid levels were lower in B. bifidum-treated syngeneic tumour mice than in anti-PD-1-alone controls, with the greatest reduction in the anti-PD-1 plus B. bifidum K57 group, consistent with a lipid-lowering effect accompanying antitumour T cell activity.

In a phase 1 FMT trial (n=10 anti-PD-1-refractory metastatic melanoma patients), B. bifidum relative abundance was lower in recipient stool post-FMT plus nivolumab versus pretreatment (ANCOM); the paper contextualizes this decrease as potentially favorable for anti-tumor immune activation, citing B. bifidum's reported role in promoting immune tolerance via induction of regulatory T cells.

In a phase 1 FMT trial (n=10 anti-PD-1-refractory metastatic melanoma patients), Bifidobacterium bifidum relative abundance was lower in recipient stool post-FMT plus nivolumab versus pretreatment (ANCOM); the paper notes that B. bifidum has been reported to promote immune tolerance via induction of regulatory T cells, framing its post-FMT decrease as potentially favorable for anti-tumor immune activation.

ClinicalAssociation.association_text: Blautia genus is significantly more depleted in adult patients with concomitant IBD and CDI than in patients with IBD alone, with the reduction in relative gut proportions more marked when CDI complicates IBD, indicating that concurrent infection compounds IBD-associated dysbiosis beyond baseline.

Blautia obeum strain A2-162 produces the lantibiotic nisin O in the human gastrointestinal tract, which exhibits direct antimicrobial activity against Clostridioides difficile; depletion of Blautia in the IBD gut may therefore remove a colonization resistance mechanism against CDI.

Blautia genus (particularly Blautia obeum) is enriched in healthy FMT donor stool and is consistently restored after successful FMT in patients with recurrent CDI, with Blautia-derived bile salt hydrolase activity negatively correlated with C. difficile spore germination, establishing it as a key restoration target for gut microbiota reconstitution.

ClinicalAssociation.association_text: Prevotella copri is enriched in the gut microbiome of healthy controls compared to patients with non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC), as identified by LEfSe analysis of 16S rRNA stool sequencing from 96 NSCLC patients versus 139 healthy controls.

Prevotella copri caused a clinically significant bloodstream infection (bacteremia) in a 90-year-old male patient with acute cardiac decompensation due to heart failure, representing the first reported case of BSI attributed to this organism; blood cultures grew P. copri as the sole pathogen and the patient recovered following treatment with metronidazole and piperacillin-tazobactam.

Roseburia-derived butyrate serves as the primary energy source for colonocytes and exerts anti-inflammatory effects by inhibiting histone deacetylases and reinforcing gut barrier integrity; depletion of Roseburia in IBD therefore represents a mechanistic loss of epithelial protection and mucosal immune regulation.

RiskContexts.risk_context: chronic H. pylori infection in gastric mucosa

ClinicalAssociation.association_text: Helicobacter pylori is an IACR-designated human carcinogen and primary cause of gastric cancer; CagA-mediated chronic inflammation of the gastric mucosa drives carcinogenesis, accounting for the majority of non-cardia gastric cancers globally. H. pylori is responsible for approximately 1 million incident cancer cases annually and eradication with antibiotic therapy reduces gastric cancer risk.

H. pylori infection is a causal driver of MALT lymphoma (B-cell marginal zone lymphoma of the stomach); antibiotic-based eradication therapy is FDA-approved as standard of care and can achieve complete remission in the majority of early-stage H. pylori-positive MALT lymphoma cases, representing a well-established example of bacterium-driven malignancy cured by antibiotics.
